ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Urology Consultation — Benjamin Franklin — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Four-week gout and blood pressure review, with urology consultation for a bladder stone

text.paragraph: Bladder stone with hematuria and obstructive voiding symptoms in a 76-year-old man with gout and stage 3a chronic kidney disease. Please confirm the diagnosis, remove the stone, look for its cause and for other sources of the bleeding, and advise on preventing recurrence. [S]

list.item: Do you confirm a bladder stone, and does it need removal now?
Is bladder outlet obstruction from the prostate the cause, and should it be treated at the same time?
Does the hematuria need further evaluation, including cystoscopy for a bladder tumor?
Is a uric acid stone probable, and what metabolic testing and prevention do you advise?
Is PSA testing needed before treatment?

text.paragraph: Mr. Franklin is seen at the request of Dr. Penhallow for a bladder stone found on CT. For several years he has had a slow stream and nocturia, and for two months an interrupted stream, pain at the end of voiding that is worse after walking or car travel, and pink urine. He has had no fever, retention, or urinary infections. He has recurrent gout and started allopurinol four weeks ago. He has never smoked and has no history of pelvic radiation or occupational dye exposure. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston on January 17, 1706 (New Style); an editor's note to his autobiography gives the date as Sunday, January 6, old style, 1706, in a house on Milk Street. [D]

In a letter of July 31, 1786, Franklin recalled that in 1724, as a compositor at Palmer's printing house in London, he sometimes heated his case of type before the fire to warm his hands, until an old workman warned him he might lose the use of his hands, and that he had felt a kind of obscure pain in the bones of his hand when working over very hot type. [D]

A 2008 review of his medical history by Finger and Hagemann concluded that he suffered repeated attacks of gout and a large bladder stone, which caused considerable pain and markedly decreased his mobility. [D]

The same review argues that several factors that raise uric acid converged in him, including sex, genetics, diet, drinking, advanced age, psoriasis, and possible lead poisoning from lead exposure. [R]

Franklin wrote the Dialogue between Franklin and the Gout, headed Midnight, October 22, 1780, in which the Gout tells him he has eaten and drunk too freely and indulged his indolence; a 2023 rheumatology review states that he woke with a gout attack that night. [D]

In a letter from Passy dated March 12, 1781, to Samuel Huntington, President of Congress, Franklin wrote that he had passed his seventy-fifth year and that the long and severe fit of the gout he had the last winter had shaken him exceedingly, leaving him far from his former bodily strength. [D]

The 1806 edition of his works states that he had been little subject to disease, except an attack of the gout occasionally, until about the year 1781, when he was first attacked with symptoms of the calculous complaint, which continued during his life. [D]
In his autobiography Franklin wrote that at the beginning of February 1726/7 he was taken ill with a pleurisy that very nearly carried him off. [D]

The 1806 edition of his works adds that in 1735 he had a severe pleurisy that ended in an abscess of the left lobe of his lungs, and that a second similar attack some years later left no lasting effect on his breathing. [D]
His autobiography records that he never knew his father or mother to have any sickness but that of which they died, his father Josiah at 89 in 1744 and his mother Abiah at 85 in 1752. [D]
Franklin wrote that in 1736 he lost a son, a boy of four, to smallpox taken in the common way, and regretted that he had not had him inoculated. [D]
A 2023 review describes him as overweight and as probably having had consequences of the metabolic syndrome, including gout. [R]

list.item: Bladder stone (N21.0). Confirmed: a single 2.6 cm stone. Its low density on CT, his acidic urine, and his gout make uric acid the probable composition. It should be removed. [S]

Bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia (N40.1). Maximum flow 8.5 mL/s, residual 160 mL, IPSS 16, and a trabeculated bladder with an obstructing median lobe. Obstruction is the probable cause of the stone, and a bladder stone caused by obstruction is an indication for surgery, so both should be treated at one operation. [S]
Hematuria. Explained by the stone; cystoscopy shows no tumor, and CT shows no kidney or ureteric lesion. Repeat urinalysis after treatment; further imaging only if hematuria persists. [S]
Chronic kidney disease G3a (N18.31). No hydronephrosis; avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic contrast around surgery. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: The non-contrast CT, intake urinalysis, serum urate and kidney function, and today's IPSS, uroflowmetry, bladder ultrasound for residual, and office flexible cystoscopy. [S]

list.item: Transurethral laser cystolitholapaxy with transurethral resection of the prostate at one operation in about three weeks; send the stone for analysis and the tissue for pathology. [S]
Tamsulosin 0.4 mg at bedtime until surgery to ease voiding. [S]
No PSA test: at 76 it would not change management, and the resected tissue will be examined. [S]
After surgery, repeat urinalysis for red cells and pH, and a 24-hour urine collection for volume, uric acid, citrate, and calcium. [S]

If the stone is uric acid: fluids for at least 2.5 L of urine a day, potassium citrate to a urine pH of 6.0 to 6.5 with potassium monitoring because of losartan and kidney disease, and continued allopurinol titration. [S]
Check IPSS and post-void residual about one, three, and six months after surgery. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Penhallow the same day; the patient agrees and asked for a written explanation of the operation. [S]

Follow-up: Urology performs the operation and the post-operative check. Primary care manages urate lowering, stone prevention, and kidney and blood pressure monitoring. Return to urology for recurrent stones, hematuria, retention, or worsening symptoms. [S]
